..
Issued at 230 PM CDT Fri Aug 14 2026

The synoptic pattern of late remains largely unchanged with
500-hPa ridging across the central CONUS. An MCV located over
eastern NE and western IA can be seen in satellite imagery and
is reflected by a weak shortwave moving through the flow. At the
surface, a stationary front remains parked across northern MO
with hot and humid conditions to the south of the boundary.
Cloud cover and scattered showers have been present through much
of the day thus far across northern MO and are tied to forcing
from the MCV and shortwave. This has helped to limit 
temperatures along and north of US-36. Cloud cover has also been
present over central MO, however, a clearing trend has been
noted over the past several hours and expectation is for
temperatures to climb into the mid-to-upper 90s this afternoon
with dew points in the mid-70s. This will result in heat indices
once again making a run towards 110F and thus the Extreme Heat
Warning and Heat Advisory remain in effect through 9 PM
Saturday. With the showers across northern MO, it is possible 
that areas in the Heat Advisory may remain below criteria today,
however, hot and humid conditions are expected again tomorrow, 
so opted to leave the advisory in effect.

The MCV is expected to track eastward across IA this afternoon
and into the overnight hours, inciting convection in central and
eastern IA this evening. Current expectation is for this
convection to follow the CAPE gradient east-southeastward
through IA, which would largely keep storms to the north of the
area. However, many of the CAMs depict storms initiating off of
the stationary front in northeastern MO as the forcing
associated with the shortwave moves through. As such, have 
opted to include a 20-40% chance of storms across northeastern 
MO through the evening and overnight hours to account for this.

If storms are able to form, they would have 2000-3000 J/kg of
MUCAPE (1000-2000 J/kg of MLCAPE south of the stationary front)
and 25-35 kts of deep layer shear to work with, so it is not 
out of the question to see organized convection overnight 
tonight across northeastern MO. The primary threats would be 
strong winds and quarter-size hail, however, with a surface 
boundary in play, a tornado or two cannot be ruled out where 
surface vorticity is maximized. Another note of concern stems 
from the 2-2.5" PWATs across northern MO. This, along with deep 
warm cloud layers, will allow storms to be very efficient 
rainfall producers and may lead to flash flooding, particularly 
if storms train along the stationary front. All of this to say, 
that any convection that is able to form across northern MO this
evening and overnight will be worth keeping an eye on.

Saturday will see more of the same with the stationary front
remaining stalled across northern MO, allowing extreme heat to
build across central MO (heat indices of 105-110F). The front 
will once again be a focal point for convection Saturday 
afternoon and evening as another weak shortwave moves overhead. 
With 2500-3500 J/kg of MLCAPE available, the primary limiting 
factor for organized convection will be deep layer shear values
of 15-20 kts. As such the primary concerns on Saturday are 
locally heavy rainfall (PWATs remain in the 2-2.5" range) and 
gusty winds. Timing remains a bit uncertain at this point, but 
the most optimal window looks to be tied to peak heating from 
mid-afternoon through the evening hours.

The stationary boundary will finally begin moving southward as a
cold front on Sunday. While Sunday will still be hot and humid
ahead of the front, this will bring much needed relief from the
oppressive conditions to the area by Monday. No heat products
have been issued for Sunday at this time as the timing of the
frontal passage will dictate how high the heat indices will get,
however, a Heat Advisory or Extreme Heat Warning may be needed
along and south of the Missouri River with future forecast
cycles.

Uncertainty in the forecast climbs as model guidance diverges 
into next week. The ECMWF and its ensemble want to build another
ridge over the central CONUS while the GFS and GEFS depict a
string of shortwaves through next week, which would result in
cooler and wetter conditions. Suffice it to say, the forecast
will need to be monitored over the coming days to see if the
relief from the heat and humidity will last or if another heat 
wave may be on the way.
